title: Channel Home Centers, Division of Grace Retail Corp. v. Grossman
summary: An agreement to negotiate in good faith is an enforceable contract if it otherwise meets contract requirements; a landlord’s signed letter-of-intent promise to withdraw the store from the market and negotiate the lease only with the prospective tenant could bind him, and the tenant’s execution of the letter, which the landlord wanted to show lenders, was consideration.

795 F.2d 291 (3d Cir. 1986). The letter of intent itself was the consideration: Channel's execution and tender of the letter, which Grossman used to obtain financing, conferred a bargained-for benefit supporting his return promise to withdraw the premises from the market and negotiate in good faith.

sections.Parties: Channel Home Centers, a home-improvement retail chain operated as a division of Grace Retail Corporation, was the prospective tenant and plaintiff. Frank Grossman, a real-estate developer, and the entities through which he was acquiring a shopping mall were the defendants. Channel sought to enforce the letter of intent and stop Grossman from leasing the space to a competitor; Grossman maintained that the letter was a nonbinding preliminary document.
sections.Material Facts: Channel became interested in leasing space, and on December 11, 1984 sent Grossman a detailed letter of intent describing a 25-year lease of about 70,400 square feet with a rent schedule and percentage rent. It stated: “To induce the Tenant to proceed with the leasing of this Store, you will withdraw the Store from the rental market, and only negotiate the above described leasing transaction to completion.” Grossman had asked for such a letter to show “other people, banks or whatever,” and promptly signed and returned it. Both sides then worked toward a lease: Channel spent about $25,000 on measurements, plans, marketing and equipment; Grossman applied for zoning permits for Channel’s signs and exchanged draft leases. On February 6, 1985 Grossman ended negotiations, asserting a 30-day deadline the letter did not contain, and on February 7 leased the space to Mr. Good Buys at substantially higher rent.
sections.Procedural History: Channel sued in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania under diversity jurisdiction and sought a preliminary injunction. The district court consolidated the injunction hearing with trial on the merits under Rule 65(a)(2) without clear advance notice and held the letter unenforceable because it did not bind the parties, lacked consideration and failed Pennsylvania’s statute of frauds for leases; it also rejected Channel’s unilateral-contract and promissory-estoppel theories. The Third Circuit (Becker, J., with Weis and Higginbotham, JJ.) reversed and remanded on June 30, 1986, 795 F.2d 291, for trial on whether the parties intended to be bound and how long the duty to negotiate lasted.
sections.Issue: Under Pennsylvania law, is a landlord’s promise in a signed letter of intent to take the premises off the market and negotiate the lease only with the prospective tenant an enforceable contract even though the lease itself remained to be negotiated? Did the parties intend to be bound by that promise, was it supported by consideration, and was it sufficiently definite?
sections.Holding: An agreement to negotiate in good faith, if it otherwise meets the requirements of a contract, is enforceable. Under Pennsylvania law that turns on whether the parties manifested an intention to be bound, whether the terms are definite enough to enforce, and whether there was consideration. The evidence would support a finding that the parties intended to be bound by Grossman’s promise to withdraw the store from the market and negotiate exclusively with Channel; the promise was definite enough to enforce; and Channel’s execution and delivery of the letter, which Grossman wanted to obtain financing, was consideration. The statute of frauds was irrelevant because Channel did not claim the letter was a lease. Reversed and remanded.
sections.Reasoning: On intent the court looked to the whole letter and the surrounding circumstances. Most of the letter described lease terms the parties plainly expected to negotiate further, but the exclusive-negotiation clause was unequivocal, and the parties’ conduct afterward, Channel’s planning expenditures, Grossman’s zoning applications for Channel’s signs and the exchange of draft leases, was consistent with a binding commitment; that evidence supported, without compelling, a finding of intent to be bound. On definiteness the court distinguished an unenforceable agreement to agree on the lease itself from Grossman’s specific, discrete undertaking to take the property off the market and negotiate exclusively, whose breach a court could identify, and held with courts elsewhere that a good-faith negotiation agreement meeting contract requirements is enforceable. On consideration Grossman had requested the letter to show lenders, and Channel’s signature, backed by its corporate parent, strengthened his financing position, so Channel’s execution and tender of the letter was a bargained-for benefit. On remand the factfinder would decide intent and duration, including whether the claimed 30-day limit had been agreed and, if not, what period was reasonable.

learning.why: This is a bargained preliminary contract. Compare Dixon and Cyberchron, which use reliance to protect narrower promises without a completed bargain.

topics.assent: The relevant assent concerns a limited negotiation obligation, not the final lease.
topics.preliminary-agreements: A signed letter can bind parties to exclusive good-faith negotiations while leaving the final deal unsettled.
topics.consideration: The requested financing value of Channel’s signed letter supplied a bargained benefit.
topics.definiteness: The withdrawal and exclusive-negotiation promises supplied content even while lease terms remained open.
topics.good-faith: Good-faith negotiation follows from the particular agreement; it is distinct from a universal duty to conclude negotiations.
topics.precontractual-liability: Channel Home is the leading case recognizing an enforceable agreement to negotiate in good faith before any final contract exists.
topics.reliance: Channel's expenditures on draft leases, plans and equipment during negotiations were central to the court's willingness to enforce the letter of intent.
